To address this limitation, Open-Vocabulary Object Detection (OVOVOD) has emerged as a solution, aiming to detect objects beyond the scope of trained categories. This area of research is still in its early stages, with existing methods heavily relying on external knowledge and labeled data. To overcome these challenges, we propose an innovative approach called Open Semantic Supervised Learning (OSSL) for OVOVOD. This approach integrates a powerful semantic model to guide the object detection process, allowing for the use of labeled data and the sharing of parameters between the two models. By leveraging these resources, OSSL significantly reduces the need for annotated data and external knowledge. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, showcasing its ability to generalize to new object categories and significantly outperform existing methods.

We've created and analyzed a comprehensive 3D model of a photodissociation region in a specific area of the L1688 cloud, characterized by a dense molecular clump and an ionizing source. The cloud's density distribution is influenced by a combination of a spherical density cusp and an external pressure envelope. Our model, which incorporates a range of physical parameters, has been compared to $A$-band interferometric data and revealed discrepancies. The cloud's density and the ionizing flux from L1688VR were estimated, and the discrepancies in the $A$-band data were attributed to a lack of three-dimensional structure in the data reduction process.

The remarkable success of Transformer models across numerous tasks has sparked significant interest in understanding the underlying mechanisms driving this success. Unfortunately, existing research primarily focuses on analyzing the behavior of these models rather than explaining it. Our work bridges this gap by developing a theoretical framework that mathematically explains why self-attention mechanisms are effective. Our approach involves creating a theoretical model based on the fundamental principles of the Transformer, and demonstrating how these mechanisms cooperate to facilitate learning within this framework. Our findings are supported by numerical experiments that showcase the practical relevance of our theoretical approach in understanding the behavior of transformers.

Mortality forecasting is a complex task that has been made more efficient through machine learning techniques. Recent studies have shown that machine ensembles can improve prediction accuracy, but they are often limited to analyzing small datasets. Our work expands on previous research by developing a machine learning ensemble framework capable of handling large datasets, such as those found in the Global Burden of Disease study. This new approach combines the outputs of multiple machine learning models to create a robust forecast. To evaluate its performance, we tested the framework on various datasets, including 189 countries' mortality data from 1990 to 2016, categorized by age and cause of death. Our results show that the proposed machine learning ensemble framework yields highly accurate and reliable forecasts, outperforming the conventional linear regression and other machine learning methods in the long term.

We've developed an innovative neural architecture search method called NAS-MAD, which focuses on minimizing interference between child models during the search process. NAS-MAD utilizes a shared operator that's selected from a large set of candidate operators, which helps reduce model interactions. Our study reveals a correlation between the level of overlap between child models and negative effects on model performance, and we measure this overlap using the Kullback-Leibler divergence. NAS-MAD uses policy-based gradient estimation to derive the gradient of the KL divergence with respect to operator selection probabilities, and then employs the cross-entropy method to adjust the probabilities. Our approach is capable of working with any operator library, and we demonstrate its effectiveness using PyNAS libraries. Our experiments show that NAS-MAD achieves better performance than state-of-the-art methods on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets, with significantly fewer evaluations.

Time series data is frequently transformed into a vector of features through a process called feature extraction, which enables the utilization of established machine learning models. This chapter examines the diverse feature extraction techniques and discusses the challenges associated with selecting features, including statistical and optimization-based methods, as well as a comprehensive example implementation in Python for each technique.
We identify concrete, infinitely precise criteria under which a proper geodesically complete CAT(0) space has a semistable fundamental group at its boundary.

This research focuses on developing a neural assessment model for translating
English into German, as it is crucial to translate quality to ensure reliable
translation output. We utilize parallel sentences from various datasets to
train the model, which can then be applied to different domains. By analyzing
the results, we discover that training the model with diverse datasets enhances
its performance in specific domains while also enabling it to perform well in
unseen domains. Furthermore, our study reveals that a model trained in a
particular domain may not be reliable for assessing translation quality in
other domains unless the translators involved have substantial experience.

In random scattering systems, the intensity at each point is determined by a matrix that defines how it is split between different paths. The matrix, known as the deposition matrix, is set up to achieve a desired intensity distribution that is resistant to changes in the path of light. The research presented here examines the properties of this matrix, revealing that it is unique and that its values are constrained by the total intensity and how it is distributed. The study also demonstrates a mathematical connection between this matrix and a problem that seeks to minimize errors in splitting intensities, and that as the number of possible paths increases, the values in the matrix tend towards an average. The findings have been experimentally verified, and that they can be used to predict and control complex light patterns in various applications.

Recent studies have shown that pruning unnecessary connections in neural networks can enhance their computational efficiency without compromising their learning capabilities. This paper investigates the characteristics of pruning methods that remove the least essential connections from neural networks, allowing the remaining ones to retain maximum functionality. Our experiments on image classification tasks reveal that the connections that remain after various pruning methods tend to form hierarchical structures, similar to those found in hierarchical neural networks. Furthermore, we discovered that different pruning methods converge to nearly identical sub-networks, regardless of their initial design. This insight led us to propose a new, straightforward pruning method that retains a small percentage of high-level connections in fully connected networks, resulting in a sub-network with significantly higher classification accuracy than the original pruned network.

In lotteries with extremely low odds of winning, people often play based on the dream of winning a jackpot. The probability of winning is often calculated using a simplified model, but this is inaccurate for multiple winners. The inclusion of this factor in the expected value of a lottery ticket can affect a player's decision, especially when playing in large groups. The probability of multiple winners is also analyzed in relation to a lottery draw, and the impact of this probability on expected value is examined through an analysis of Powerball. The probability of two winners is found to be significant enough to affect expected value in certain cases. The probability of more than one winner is also calculated using the simplified model, and the effect of this probability on expected value is examined through an analysis of Powerball. The probability of two winners is found to be significant enough to affect expected value in certain cases.

The complete set of $N_f^4$ contributions to the anomalous dimensions of twist-two operators at the six-loop level in $QCD$ has been calculated using the next-to-leading double-logarithmic evolution kernel. This was achieved by adapting the light-ray operator product expansion and conformal bootstrap approaches, which enabled the inclusion of previously overlooked contributions involving operators with five or more legs. These contributions are crucial for accurately determining the leading logarithmic terms. Additionally, the study's findings were cross-verified with recent results from the conformal bootstrap.

Two-dimensional materials exhibit unique properties in valley physics, which can be manipulated through mechanical strain. However, research on the valley Hall effect in static and dynamic strain environments has been limited. In this study, we investigate the valley Hall responses under conditions of dynamic strain and find that certain frequencies can induce or suppress these responses. Specifically, we identify frequencies where valley Hall conductances are maximized or entirely quenched. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the ratio between these responses can be controlled by adjusting the valley Hall angle, which is highly sensitive to both static and dynamic strain.

The domain shift issue has long plagued deep learning applications in remote sensing, a problem that domain adaptation methods have attempted to mitigate. The unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) methods, despite their potential, have been hindered by the need for accurate pseudo-labels generation. This limitation can be overcome by incorporating self-training techniques, a technique that has been widely used in vision tasks but has not been extensively explored in remote sensing applications. This paper proposes a novel self-training approach, STUda, that effectively tackles the domain shift problem in urban building detection, a challenging remote sensing application. The method, which requires no pseudo-labels, leverages a novel uncertainty-aware pseudo-label generation technique to mitigate the negative effects of mislabeled data. The extensive experiments conducted on three publicly available remote sensing datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of STUda, outperforming existing state-of-the-art UDA methods.

The t-SNE algorithm has become a widely used dimensionality reduction technique for visualizing complex data patterns. By focusing on local similarities within t-distributed projections, t-SNE has surpassed other methods that rely on uniform distributions. Despite its effectiveness, t-SNE's theoretical underpinnings remain unclear, particularly regarding the nature of its t-distribution and its impact on dimensionality reduction outcomes. This study investigates how the t-SNE method behaves under different conditions, such as varying numbers of dimensions and different values of stochasticity, and provides new insights into its sensitivity to these factors.

We have developed an approach to study the two-dimensional Fermi polaron model, which is based on the Bethe ansatz. This approach enables us to investigate how the system behaves at different interaction strengths between the impurity and the Fermi sea. We have found that the model exhibits a broad range of phase transitions, which can be explained by a single function that is valid across all interaction strengths. This result is consistent with previous studies that used the variational method and supports the idea that there is a ground state transition from bound polaron to dressed impurity as the interaction strength increases.

In this paper, we propose the application of digital-analog quantum computing to model the ground state energy of fermionic systems, focusing on the Heisenberg model. We identify the ideal qubit network structure as an n-qubit system for simulating the growth of the ground state energy of non-interacting fermions in one dimension. We demonstrate that digital-analog quantum computing can be used to efficiently calculate the ground state energy of non-interacting fermions in a two-dimensional square lattice with arbitrary site occupancy. We also show that the method can be applied to simulate the ground state energy of fermions in arbitrary confined potentials. Furthermore, we provide an in-depth analysis of the advantages of using digital-analog quantum computing over other methods, such as randomized measurements, in terms of circuit depth and resource requirements.

Graph polynomials, including the chromatic polynomial, have been extensively studied due to their connection to various graph properties. The evaluation of the chromatic polynomial at -1 reveals the count of a graph's spanning subgraphs with two colorings. This research focuses on identifying properties that can be counted by evaluating a multivariate polynomial, defined for any graph G and integers k and l, at a specific point. The developed polynomial evaluates to a sum of (-1) raised to the power of a spanning subgraph's edges count, multiplied by k times (a factor representing the number of connected components minus one) and l times (the sum of a factor representing the number of connected components minus one). This polynomial generalizes properties such as spanning subgraphs count, their distribution by connected components, and their distribution by the number of connected components, as well as a new property. The research also demonstrates that this polynomial can be expressed as a sum over all possible partitions of a graph's vertex set, multiplied by (-1) raised to a higher power, and includes a description of the resulting quantity. This generalization is achieved by proving that the polynomial can be expressed as a sum over all possible partitions of a graph's vertex set, multiplied by (-1) raised to a higher power, and includes the number of complete subgraphs in each partition. This development is further explored by evaluating the polynomial for special classes of graphs, such as trees, complete graphs, and complete multipartite graphs, and also generalizations

We derive an expression for the pullback of the Hitchin connection, extending from the moduli space of curves of genus g to a holomorphic affine bundle over the Teichmuller bundle, which includes all possible pairs of a Riemann surface of genus g and a non-zero meromorphic 1-form w. This expression is represented as a limit when g approaches infinity, utilizing a sequence of genera g_n = n.

The COVID-19 pandemic has forced many workers to adapt to remote work, which has been shown to boost employee well-being, but the type of support provided is crucial in achieving this goal. Our study, which involved 111 participants from 17 companies in Italy, investigated the support available during the pandemic. Using a survey, we analyzed data on different forms of support, including instrumental, emotional, and informational assistance, and found a link between support and employee well-being. Our analysis revealed that companies should prioritize emotional support to improve employee well-being, and that organizations offering emotional and relational support have a higher likelihood of retaining workers.

The concept of dichotomous matrices serves as an extension of Hermitian matrices, with specific relationships existing among these types, as well as with real symmetric and complex symmetric matrices, facilitated by a mapping. A natural question arises regarding the correspondence between linearly invariant subspaces of dichotomous matrices and their real symmetric counterparts. In this study, we establish a connection between the spectra of real symmetric matrices and their associated dichotomous matrices, as well as an exploration of the relationships among their invariant subspaces.

In a study of in-variant-mass-distributed electrons originating from beauty hadron decays in Pb-Pb collisions at 5.02 TeV, invariant-mass-selected electrons in Pb-Pb and p-Pb collisions were analyzed using ALICE data. These electrons were measured within the rapidity range of -0.7 < y < 0.7 and transverse momentum range of 2-100 GeV/c. For Pb-Pb collisions, correction factors for nuclear modifications and cold nuclear matter effects were applied to invariant-momentum-selected electrons in p-Pb collisions to compare them with their Pb-Pb counterparts. These selected electrons exhibit a characteristic $v_2$ pattern, indicating $v_2$ of in-beauty hadrons. A distinct $v_2$ behavior was observed for low-momentum beauty hadrons ($p_T < 10$ GeV/c), while those with higher momentum showed a lack of $v_2$, suggesting that in the medium, high-momentum beauty quarks experience reduced interactions.

In this paper, we identify conditions that lead to broad conclusions about chromatic sets, a concept that has gained interest in recent research. This concept is a variation of the classic (finite) chromatic number, and our study confirms previous findings by Gerber et al. and Lutz et al. as well as yielding new results that apply to subsets of n-dimensional Euclidean space, as well as subsets of a metric measure space.

In this study, we investigate the relationship between the number of users and the maximum achievable gain from optimal power control in massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems. A large-scale MIMO system is defined as one where the number of antenna elements far exceeds the number of users. We develop an analytical model for optimal power control in such systems, showing that its extremal power control gain increases linearly with the number of users. This model is then validated through extensive numerical simulations. Furthermore, we establish a maximum power control gain threshold for optimal power control in large-scale MIMO systems, which approaches a specific constant value as the number of users increases.

This paper presents a novel approach to categorization with clear explanations, which is highly relevant to the extensive volume of categorization tasks in auditing. The method combines techniques from data mining and graph theory to generate categorization rules that are easily understandable. The proposed algorithm, X-CAT, is a rule-based method that identifies categories by iteratively selecting items based on their ability to explain other items. The key feature of X-CAT is its ability to provide clear explanations for categorization decisions, a trait highly valued in areas like healthcare and auditing. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through an application to audit working papers, resulting in a set of interpretable categorization rules that can be used to improve the categorization process. The results show that X-CAT outperforms traditional machine learning methods in terms of interpretability and overall performance.

The Strauss process, with a given intensity and points within a certain distance contributing to its density, is being analyzed in this research. We derive an expression for its specific density function and examine the conditions for this density to reach its maximum value. This examination leads us to identify the parameters under which the Strauss process exhibits a phase transition, with the implications being that such a transition does not occur.

In the context of string theory and quantum gravity, the Generalized Uncertainty Principle (GUP) indicates the presence of a fundamental scale in nature. Our research explores the implications of GUP within the framework of the string worldsheet, incorporating a string scale cutoff. We derive the string version of GUP, $\Delta x \Delta p \geq \hbar/2$ $(\alpha_s \Delta p^2 + \beta_s \Delta x^2)^{1/2}$, where $\alpha_s$ and $\beta_s$ are constants related to the string scale. Notably, the recovery of the standard uncertainty relation occurs when $\alpha_s = 0$, and the new relationship between coordinates and momenta arises from $\beta_s$. Our analysis reveals that the GUP on the string worldsheet is equivalent to the spacetime GUP, $\Delta x \Delta p \geq \hbar/2$ $(l_p^2 \Delta x^2)^{1/2}$, where $l_p$ is the Planck length.

Multitasking scheduling in cloud computing systems is crucial for efficiently utilizing computing resources. The objective of this scheduling problem is to minimize makespan, which represents the time required to complete a task and move on to the next one. To achieve this goal, a task must be assigned to a processor and then executed. Following task assignment, the system must either migrate or not migrate the task, depending on whether a processor change occurs. Our proposed algorithm, called Multitasking Scheduling with Migration Decision (MSMD), is an approximation approach that minimizes makespan in constant time. It works by first using a greedy algorithm to assign tasks to processors and then deciding if task migration is necessary. The results show that MSMD achieves a constant approximation ratio of 4.5.

Developing robust controllers for legged robots to navigate and adapt to the ever-changing terrain of natural environments remains a significant challenge in the field of legged locomotion. The diverse terrain types found in nature, characterized by their distinct physical properties, can be grouped into a few distinct categories based on their hardness and deformation characteristics. In this paper, we introduce a field-guided legged locomotion controller designed to facilitate the seamless transition between different types of locomotion strategies, enabling a quadruped robot to efficiently traverse and adapt to various ground conditions. The proposed controller, which is parameterized and trained using reinforcement learning, incorporates a unique feature that allows for the controlled manipulation of its internal states, thus facilitating the transition between different modes of locomotion. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through simulations, which show its ability to adapt to different terrain types and outperform existing controllers in various scenarios.

The proliferation of the Internet of Things (IoT) has led to a significant increase in the number of IoT devices, driving a surge in network traffic. To accommodate this, major telecom operators are rapidly deploying IoT networks, including NB-IoT and MTC, to support a vast array of devices. As these networks are rolled out in phases, operators often introduce firmware updates to optimize performance. However, such updates can disrupt service, negatively impacting the Quality of Service (QoS) of existing IoT networks. To mitigate this, operators typically execute firmware upgrades in stages, allowing for the assessment of associated QoS risks. This study presents a comprehensive framework for analyzing QoS Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) in IoT networks during these firmware upgrades, with a focus on a real-world case study of a major telecom operator's 4G NB-IoT network in India. The analysis encompasses various QoS KPIs, including connection success rates, data transmission rates, and network latency.

We've developed a method to calculate the local Fock space self-energy's imaginary component for non-interacting and many-body localized systems with binary disorder. This approach is based on a Taylor series expansion of the localized eigenstates around the initial state, enabling us to establish an upper limit on the imaginary part's growth rate with increasing number of basis states. We've also derived precise expressions for the local self-energy's real and imaginary parts at the lowest order term.

A new variant of the interactive graph search problem, kBM-IGS, is a budgeted model that aims to find k disjoint vertex sets of minimum size, where each set ensures a minimum balance of red and blue neighbors for a designated query vertex. This problem is an iterative model that incorporates query-based feedback. We've established that kBM-IGS is NP-hard and designed an approximation algorithm with a constant-factor performance guarantee. We also explored the relationship between kBM-IGS and the kBM-ICG problem, which is a non-interactive graph classification problem. By reducing kBM-ICG to kBM-IGS, we demonstrated that solving the interactive graph classification problem can lead to significant improvements in approximation quality for kBM-IGS.

The rapid advancement of quantum technology has generated considerable interest in the potential for quantum computers to revolutionize various fields, including machine learning. Despite the theoretical understanding that quantum computers might solve specific machine learning tasks exponentially faster than classical computers, a detailed analysis of the associated requirements remains missing. In this study, we investigate the necessary quantum resources to implement a particular quantum version of support vector machines. We find that for this algorithm to achieve exponential speedup, it must utilize a specific quantum data encoding that can also be viewed as a kernel function. This highly expressive kernel enables the separation of complex datasets, but also risks overfitting. In contrast, most existing quantum machine learning models lack explicit data encoding and instead rely on inputting training data sequentially. However, these models cannot achieve exponential speedup. Our study provides valuable insights into the trade-offs between quantum resource requirements and potential speedup in quantum-enhanced machine learning.

We investigate Steklov eigenvalues in nearly spherical three-dimensional domains under various domain perturbations, establishing their differentiability, asymptotic expansion, and the three-ball inequality.

Conformance checking focuses on comparing process models to actual event data, and alignment techniques are essential tools in this field. A key objective of alignments is to establish a direct correlation between process model transitions and observed events, and recent advancements have led to the development of automated alignment generation methods. This paper presents a novel approach to creating alignments by utilizing sequence pattern mining, and our method excels in several key aspects compared to existing techniques, including achieving state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks, producing a smaller number of alignments for a process execution, and enabling users to incorporate domain-specific knowledge to guide alignment discovery.

Accurate prediction of radio propagation is essential for modern mobile networks, which rely heavily on seamless connectivity. This is particularly crucial in urban environments, where buildings obstruct and scatter radio signals. This paper examines the differences between models based on statistical data and those that use deterministic methods, which can be either empirical or predictive. It also explores the trade-offs between accuracy and computational efficiency, and provides an overview of the datasets used to validate these models.

A straightforward semantics is proposed for temporal planning. We define and formally establish the logic within the interactive theorem prover Isabelle/HOL, and then obtain a validation algorithm for the generated semantics using theorem proving. We also show that the validated planning problem can be solved using existing off-the-shelf planning tools.

Power system models are used to analyze and understand the complex interactions within a power grid. These models are based on a set of parameters that can vary, affecting the model's outcomes. To ensure a model's reliability, it is essential to understand which parameters have the most significant impact on the results. This study employs global sensitivity analysis to identify the parameters that influence the model's behavior. By applying a Sobol' variance-based method, we found that model structure is more important than specific parameter values. Furthermore, we found that certain key parameters, such as those related to renewable energy sources and peak energy times, have the most significant impact. This study provides valuable insights for power system planners and operators, helping them to prioritize which parameters to focus on when developing and refining their models.

This study establishes the global existence of classical solutions for the Vlasov-Poisson and the ionic Vlasov-Poisson models within bounded domains under various boundary conditions. It accommodates a wide range of boundary conditions, including reflective and non-reflective scenarios for the transport equation in the Vlasov component, as well as Dirichlet and Neumann conditions for the Poisson equation.

In the software industry, software developers and managers typically receive change requests in natural language, which they then interpret and translate into technical specifications for implementation. The requests often lack a standardized structure, making it difficult to extract precise information. Our study focuses on structured technical documentation of military software systems, which we found to be a reliable source for generating well-structured, albeit outdated, technical descriptions. The main objective of our research is to investigate the feasibility of automatically converting these technical descriptions into abstracts of requirements, which we found to be a valuable process. The resulting requirement summaries can be further translated into executable code, a task that is also explored in our research.

Our study explores the rheological characteristics of colloidal gel networks under ultrasonic vibrations, revealing that these vibrations can significantly alter a gel's viscoelastic properties. This transformation is understood as an ultrasonic-induced transition from a solid-like to a liquid-like state in the colloidal gel. Furthermore, we investigate the efficiency of ultrasonication in repacking the gel network and discover that its impact diminishes beyond a certain duration. Notably, the effectiveness of ultrasonication varies according to the gel's structural attributes, particularly the size of its colloidal particles.

This research paper explores the validity of the Collatz conjecture for a particular subset of the natural numbers, specifically those of the form $4k+1$, and in doing so, aims to ultimately prove the entire conjecture.

This paper introduces a substantial, high-quality dataset for use in processing STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) document collections, with a focus on classifying mathematical and physics-related content. We outline the process of creating a dataset for such classification, employing a fine-tuned version of the BERT model. Our benchmarking results demonstrate the superiority of this new BERT variant over traditional LSTM and CNN models. Furthermore, the dataset and related materials are made freely available to facilitate further research in this field.

Classic stable matching problems, such as the hospital residents assignment and the kidney exchange, often face challenges due to extensive preference lists.  To address this issue, we examine the impact of limiting preference lists on market stability.  By introducing a stable matching criterion for markets with restricted preference lists and proposing an axiomatic foundation, we find that this limited approach to stability corresponds with key market characteristics.  Consequently, traditional methods for ensuring stability in markets with infinite assignment capacities can be viewed as sequential applications of our new market-based stability concept.  To further illustrate this relationship, we apply our findings to the kidney exchange market, where we also propose and evaluate various methods for limiting preference lists.

Current evaluation methods for summarization models are limited by their reliance on manually annotated data or a lack of a reliable reference standard. A novel approach is proposed to address this challenge by automatically generating acceptable summaries through controlled diversity constraints and using them to develop a comprehensive evaluation metric called SummScore. This metric assesses four key dimensions of summary quality: coherence, completeness, consistency, and conciseness. Through thorough experimentation, it has been demonstrated that SummScore accurately reflects the varying qualities of summaries within a paraphrase ranking task. Furthermore, the proposed method is found to be a reliable indicator of human and neural model performance in abstract summarization tasks.

This study introduces a new approach to recover the signal covariance matrix from cross-correlation measurements, which is particularly useful in directional microphones and similar systems. The proposed method assumes that the diagonal of the cross-correlation matrix is accessible and focuses on determining a single column of the signal realization. By reducing the number of required measurements and enabling parallel processing, this technique offers a more efficient solution. Theoretical analysis and simulation results validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

This paper introduces a novel, inexpensive, and straightforward method to generate 3D object detection data for training purposes. The proposed method utilizes a camera to acquire images of scenes containing objects, and then employs simple geometric computations to convert image-based detection results into 3d-bounding-box format. 3d-bounding-box can supplement LiDAR data for training purposes, particularly in situations where LiDAR fails but a camera still functions. The proposed method is versatile and can be applied to various setups, including multiple cameras arranged in different configurations. The method's adaptability also allows it to work with single cameras. The proposed method's feasibility is demonstrated through a case study involving a single camera. The potential of the proposed method is further validated through experiments using generated data from this method, showing that the method's detection accuracy is comparable to that of real-world LiDAR data.

We have derived a new expression for the Kolmogorov length, $\eta$, which is the scale at which turbulence in a fluid becomes dominated by thermal fluctuations. This length scale is relevant to incompressible fluids and was found to be consistent with previous results for water. Our derivation is based on a different approach than earlier results, which relied on the Landau-Lifshitz theory of thermal fluctuations. Instead, we have used the equations of ideal hydrodynamics and showed that the thermal contribution to enstrophy can be obtained by considering the energy of acoustic waves in a compressible fluid. This approach led to a new expression for the thermal contribution to kinetic energy which is consistent with previous results. Our derivation also reveals that the thermal contribution to enstrophy can be obtained from the thermal contribution to kinetic energy by considering the relationship between velocity and vorticity. This new expression for the thermal contribution to enstrophy has been used to derive a new expression for the Kolmogorov length, which is given by $\eta \sim \nu^3/\epsilon^{3/4}$. This new expression is relevant to a wide range of incompressible fluids and is relevant to a wide range of turbulent flows.

In this study, we examine how thermal effects influence the propagation of laser pulses in a liquid. We establish and solve the equations governing the interaction between the laser and the liquid, and then compare our results with the common assumption that the liquid remains stationary. Our findings reveal that the liquid's movement significantly impacts laser propagation, and in the case of heat transfer, the movement can lead to enhanced energy transfer over a certain distance.

In software development, reusing past experiences is a crucial factor for success, and one way to achieve this is through experience mining. This process, also known as design mining, involves extracting valuable information from existing documentation. This paper examines the current state of experience mining in software engineering research, examining multiple studies and providing a comprehensive analysis. A key finding is that design mining has been a significant area of study, with a focus on specific design elements such as use cases, classes, and methods. This paper also outlines future research directions and challenges in the field.

The rise of big data and the Internet of Things has led to a surge in complex and expansive stream applications. To address this, stream processing systems have evolved to support diverse data sources, processing methods, and output formats. To accommodate the expanding scale of these systems, micro-services have become a crucial component, enabling them to be distributed across multiple nodes. This paper examines the key requirements for stream processing applications and the micro-services architecture, and then compares various approaches to building micro-based stream processing systems. Finally, the review identifies areas for future research and development in this field.

The search for vector-like quark partners is being conducted with the aim of discovering new physics beyond the Standard Model. These theoretical particles, specifically vector-like $T$ partners, can be produced in pairs at the Large Hadron Collider. An investigation into the production of $V$-spin doublets has been carried out, focusing on the $WZ$-associated production of $ttbar$ and the $tch$ associated production at a 13 TeV LHC with a 139 fb$^{-1}$ dataset. An analysis of these search channels found no signs of these vector-like quark partners, and as a result, upper limits on their production cross-sections have been established. These results, compared to the predicted cross-section of the Standard Model, allow for the derivation of constraints on the mass of $V$-spin doublets and their ttbar mixing angle.

Machine-translation based approaches to Neural Machine Translation (NMT) have shown promise in generating natural language to formal language pairs. However, when it comes to NMT for SPARQL, several challenges arise. Firstly, the vast range of possible generated queries makes it difficult to achieve high precision, as many valid queries can be produced for a single input. Secondly, due to SPARQL's limited syntax, a high precision rate is not a reliable indicator of whether a query conveys the correct meaning. To address these issues, we suggest a new method for Neural Machine Translation that learns to generate queries matching a reference query's semantics rather than simply translating the input text. This approach significantly improves the quality of generated queries, achieving a 10% increase in exact match precision and 5% improvement in ranked-match precision for a sample dataset.

This research introduces a novel approach to assess the quality of academic publications from both individual authors and institutional perspectives. Building on the quality metrics established in 2016, our method leverages the inherent value of specific publication venues to provide a more nuanced evaluation. To achieve this, we employ two distinct methods for calculating venue scores, considering both historical patterns and the dynamic nature of different publication venues across various fields. Furthermore, our approach allows for customization to cater to the specific needs of different stakeholders by fine-turing a primary control variable. Through a case study, we demonstrate the utility of our method in measuring the impact of open access publication policies.

The effectiveness of neural networks in approximating complex functions has made them a popular choice for designing control systems. However, identifying whether these networks satisfy safety requirements remains a challenging issue. This study introduces a precise algorithm for verifying the safety of control systems that use neural networks, enabling users to guarantee that complex models adhere to complex safety constraints. The approach leverages the fact that neural network safety verification can be reduced to a series of complex optimization problems, which are then solved using advanced optimization techniques. The results of numerical experiments demonstrate that our method can efficiently verify the safety of control systems with neural networks, even in cases involving high-dimensional state spaces and complex constraints.

Several prominent dissimilarity-based clustering theories draw inspiration from set theory, metric space, and order theory. Building on these foundations, a comprehensive framework is developed to unify and generalize the field of dissimilarity-based clustering. This framework incorporates and expands upon existing methods, presenting a novel approach to clustering. Through this lens, numerous pre-existing algorithms are reinterpreted, illustrating how their dissimilarity-based components can be substituted with more generalised methods without altering the overall clustering process. Furthermore, this framework facilitates the creation of new clustering methods by integrating novel dissimilarity-based operations.

Tensor completion is a crucial task in recovering lost data in visual information, 
involving a large number of parameters and a need for accurate predictions. 
A recent advancement, the isotropic regression manifold (IRM), has been made to address this issue. 
However, it is limited to data with missing components. 
In this paper, we develop a new approach, the Non-isotropic Regression Manifold (NRM), 
which extends IRM to handle corrupted data through a Non-isotropic Regression Manifold (NRM). 
NRM introduces new mathematical operators and a non-isotropic regression tensor to handle noise. 
We also propose an efficient algorithm to solve the underlying optimization problem. 
Our results show that NRM outperforms existing methods in completing tensors with noise corruption.

It is demonstrated that the conjugation dual algebra, consisting of Yetter-Drinfeld modules over classical Weyl groups $S_n$, yields a finite-dimensional algebra with a rich structure. This results in the creation of an ideal within the center of the algebra, leading to significant implications for representation theory. Specifically, it allows for the construction of multiple nonisomorphic simple modules over the algebra, with a parameterized family based on a variable $q$. Furthermore, a key theorem, analogous to Deligne's theorem, establishes that only certain $S_n$ lie in the algebra, with $n$ growing linearly as function of $q$.

The three-dimensional rotating system's turbulence is analyzed in the context of the barotropic quasi-geostrophic equation, which is solved using direct numerical simulations in periodic boxes at high Reynolds numbers (ranging from 2000 to 10000). The resulting flow characteristics are compared to both geostrophic turbulence and wave turbulence models to determine the primary turbulence state. The results show that the system exhibits wave turbulence characteristics, with the spectral energy distribution following the $k^{-11/3}$ scaling law, and the inverse energy cascade following the $k^{-3}$ scaling law, in agreement with theoretical predictions. The analysis reveals that the system's flow characteristics are not solely determined by Reynolds number, with the emergence of wave turbulence occurring at a specific Reynolds number (Re_c ≈ 2000). The observed features of wave turbulence, such as the presence of coherent structures, are found to be more pronounced at higher Reynolds numbers.

In the context of graph normalization, specifically the query containment problem, a crucial step is eliminating certain patterns called full cycles through a process called iterative graph normalization. Research has shown that a graph is free of full cycles if and only if its structure, when analyzed through a specific mathematical method, does not contain a specific pattern. Our study expands on previous work by considering a more general version of the process, which leads to a new characterization of graphs lacking full cycles. This characterization involves interpreting the outcome of the more general process as a sequence of specific transformations, which in turn helps in understanding the structure of the graphs involved. Our findings also have implications for the containment problem in general graphs, which in some cases can be reduced to a containment problem in graphs lacking the specific pattern.

This research investigates the impact of a magnetic field on the thermodynamic properties of a graphene system that is controlled by an electric current, in addition to a uniform magnetic field. The study compares the thermodynamic behavior of this graphene system to that of a traditional two-dimensional electron gas. The system is analyzed in the absence of scattering, with the findings indicating that the system exhibits no increase in entropy or heat capacity when exposed to the coexistence of electric and magnetic fields. The results demonstrate that the system's response to the combined fields is not passive, with the possibility of heat being converted into electrical work without any external input.

A planetary system detected in the 2017-2018 period, located at 140.3 MHz, exhibited radio emissions that hinted at magnetospheric processes within its planetary system. The emission's circular polarization indicated the presence of a magnetic field, but the emission's intensity was lower than expected for a compact source. The detection occurred during a radio burst lasting 1.5 hours, which was not predicted by the emission's characteristics. The radio burst's spectral index was calculated at -0.7, and the radio emission's flux density was calculated at 1.2 Jy. The radio emissions' properties were compared to those of other known planetary systems, and the radio emissions' properties were found to be similar to those of a hot Jupiter. This research introduces Articulated Neural Rendering (ANR), a method for generating photorealistic images of virtual human avatars in complex environments. ANR combines a neural appearance model tied to a human body mesh with a differentiable rendering process that optimizes the mesh against neural image outputs. By incorporating a message passing network, ANR efficiently handles the large-scale optimization of the mesh shape, resulting in accurate shape and pose estimations. This method allows the generated avatar to naturally interact with 3D objects and produce realistic images in various settings.

Recent breakthroughs in artificial neural networks (ANNs) have led to remarkable advancements in object recognition, outperforming humans in many benchmark tests. However, ANNs often lack the ability to replicate human visual perception, which is characterized by robustness against image distortions and the ability to focus on key features. This paper proposes a new framework for modeling human visual attention, which identifies the most critical areas of an image to achieve optimal recognition performance. The framework is applied to an object classification task using a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and demonstrates a significant improvement in performance compared to standard CNNs, particularly under severe image distortions. The results suggest that our approach can enhance the objects classification performance and may contribute to a better understanding of human visual perception.

The connection between the Askey-Wilson algebra and certain link invariants is examined in the context of three-dimensional Chern-Simons theory.  This connection is derived by representing the link invariants defined through Chern-Simons theory in terms of a representation of the AW algebra.

This study presents computational predictions for a two-dimensional kagome lattice model with a specific heat capacity and Kelland interactions. The model describes an anisotropic system with distinct horizontal and vertical bond strengths. As the system approaches quantum criticality, the model predicts a phase transition from a paramagnetic state to a long-range ordered ferromagnetic state. The model's phase diagram and thermal properties were determined using a mean-field approximation. The results indicate a two-peak structure in the specific heat, with the peaks shifting and merging as the system approaches criticality. The model's predictions are relevant for studying magnetic properties in materials like kagome magnets and Kelland models.

We introduce meta-tuning, a novel approach to enhance language models' zero-shot learning capabilities by training on a diverse set of datasets with distinct tasks. This strategy diverges from traditional few-shot learning methods in its focus on generalizing across various downstream tasks. We apply meta-tuning to the T5 model, training it on a collection of T5 datasets to create a versatile model. This model, when fine-tuned with a small number of examples on new T5 datasets, shows significant improvements of up to 12% in accuracy. Moreover, when applied to other models like BART and RoBERTa, as well as to natural language inference datasets, meta-tuning consistently yields performance gains.

In the context of the Minimal Standard Model extended with a triplet Higgs, we have conducted an electroweak baryogenesis analysis. The investigation revealed that a strong first-order electroweak phase transition is achievable, which in turn facilitates a non-zero sphaleron asymmetry and is compatible with existing data. Furthermore, we have examined the impact of various Higgs masses on the generated baryon asymmetry, as well as the effect of gauge bosons' influence during the symmetry breaking process.

We developed an innovative approach to identify reliable redshifts in the submillimeter spectrum by employing a sophisticated deep learning model that integrates a unique optimization technique to overcome convergence issues in traditional training methods. This method, stochastic layer training, enhances the training efficiency by randomly disabling a portion of network layers in each iteration. Utilizing a comprehensive dataset of 100,000 emission lines in the submillimeter range, we tested our approach and found that the resulting neural network successfully achieved a 99.9% accuracy in predicting robust single-emission-line sources. Furthermore, the network demonstrated exceptional performance in pinpointing multiple emission lines within a single source, achieving an 80% detection rate. This approach outperforms existing methods in both speed and accuracy, making it a promising tool for the analysis of large-scale submillimeter surveys.

We investigate the low-energy spin excitations in a $J_1-J_2$ Heisenberg model on a triangular lattice, where the $J_2$ term induces an ordered phase with $120^\circ$ arrangement of spins. Utilizing the linear spin wave theory, we derive a $6\times6$ dynamical spin susceptibility matrix, which allows us to compute the spectral function. This approach enables the calculation of the momentum-dependent spectral function, although it is known to have a positive-definite nature. To address this, we propose a model for the experimental spectral function based on the relationship between susceptibility and spin fluctuations. This involves a convolution of the spectral function with a Gaussian distribution, centered at magnetic wave vectors associated with different spin correlations. This model is in agreement with previous studies on $120^\circ$ ordered systems. Furthermore, we apply this model to interpret the momentum-dependent spectral function observed in $YbTi_2O_5$ through inelastic neutron scattering, and demonstrate that it can be described by the $YbTi_2O_5$'s $120^\circ$-ordered phase with spectral functions centered at specific wave vectors.

The phase structure of a non-Abelian lattice Higgs theory, specifically SU(3) Higgs with a lattice scalar field, is being studied in detail. The theory is analyzed in the Euclidean spacetime lattice, where an additional real scalar field $\beta_s$ controls the Higgs potential. The study focuses on the phase structure in the $\beta$ and $\beta_s$ plane, where $\beta$ controls the deconfinement transition. The results show that the first-order confinement-deconfinement transition occurs at $\beta_c$ when the lattice has two temporal sites and becomes a crossover when it has three temporal sites. The investigation uses Monte Carlo simulations to investigate the theory's phase structure, and the results suggest that the Higgs field's expectation value becomes non-zero in the deconfined phase, similar to what is observed in the SU(3) lattice gauge-Higgs theory.

Cr$_2$Al, a member of the Cr$_2T$ family, displays an unusual antiferromagnetic order, which can be attributed to its intricate crystal structure. The compound exhibits a n\'eel temperature of 285 K, along with a series of magnetic phase transitions that are influenced by an external magnetic field. The compound's unusual properties have been studied through the analysis of its resistivity, muon spin relaxation, and neutron diffraction. The results indicate that Cr$_2T$ compounds possess a unique magnetic structure, characterized by a combination of two- and three-dimensional ordering. The compound's magnetic behavior has been further investigated using muon spin rotation and relaxation measurements, which have revealed that its magnetic moments are aligned in a complex, three-dimensional pattern. The compound's unusual properties make it a promising candidate for the development of new spintronic devices, which could be used in the field of data storage and processing.

A new kinetic model, the $
u$-model, is introduced to simulate rarefied flows of monatomic gas, combining the simplicity of the BGK model with the precision of the Boltzmann model. This kinetic model incorporates the collision frequency $
u$, a crucial component in plasma physics, into the monatomic gas kinetic equation. By approximating the complex Boltzmann collision integral with $
u$, the $
u$-model simplifies the computational process while maintaining a reasonable level of accuracy. Specifically, the $
u$-model has been shown to yield results that closely match the Boltzmann model for high-Mach number re-entry vehicles, making it a useful tool for simulating such complex flows.

Voice assistants such as Alexa and Google Assistant benefit greatly from semantic parsing, a process that is often based on supervised learning. However, this process is hindered by the scarcity of labeled data, a problem that can be addressed through the use of data augmentation. In this study, we present an innovative, unsupervised method for enhancing semantic parsing via sentence paraphrasing, a technique that we call Semantic Parse Data Augmentation (SPDA). By leveraging meaning representations, our approach generates paraphrases with the ability to preserve the ability to identify entities and verbs. When applied to the task of identifying entities, our method yields a significant 10.5% improvement in F1 score on theontonflicks dataset. Furthermore, when combined with existing data augmentation techniques, our method yields substantial gains in both entity and verb identification performance.

The Electron-Ion Collider's future will involve a significant contribution from heavy flavor data, which can greatly enhance our understanding of particle interactions. Past research on parton distribution functions has relied on data from ep and pp collisions, but the latter cannot access the large-x region of the gluon. Measurements of gluon-favored processes in the future Electron-Ion Collider will provide crucial insights into the behavior of gluons. Furthermore, future proton-proton collisions at the same collider will enable precise measurements of inclusive and fragmentation functions using heavy flavor probes.

A new type of phenomenon called Quasi-Periodic Eruptions (QPEs) was first observed in the center of the galaxy M81 in 2016. The QPEs exhibit a periodicity of about 10-20 minutes and are characterized by a significant increase in X-ray flux. The eruptions are thought to be caused by the interaction between an orbiting object and the hot plasma in the galaxy's core. The QPEs are similar to Quasi-Periodic Oscillations (QPOs) observed in accretion disks around black holes, but they are much more energetic and involve the ejection of hot plasma. The QPEs are thought to be caused by an object of mass about 10-100 solar masses that is in a stable orbit around the black hole. The object is thought to be a neutron star or a black hole. The QPEs are thought to be caused by the interaction between the object and the hot plasma in the galaxy's core. The existence of magnetic fields in stars is essential for the generation of their energy output and the transport of angular momentum. Our understanding of these fields in solar-type stars is largely based on the detection of magnetic fields in their atmospheres through various observational methods. However, current models of non-magnetic stellar structures suggest that these fields should persist throughout the entire interior of the star, maintaining a uniform strength. In contrast, the relationship between surface magnetic fields and those in the interior remains unclear, as interior fields are not directly observable. This study examines the potential effects of varying the strength of magnetic fields with altitude in Proxima Centauri, a nearby star that hosts a planetary system and is the closest star to Earth. Our findings indicate that the star's rapid rotation and the presence of observed surface magnetic fields are consistent with an interior dynamo mechanism. This mechanism would naturally lead to variations in the magnetic field strength with altitude, as observed in the Sun. Our results also show that this interior dynamo mechanism would generate sufficient levels of convective turbulence to prevent the complete penetration of magnetic fields into the star's core.

A link exists between a Dunkl operator over a field with two elements and a first derivative, 
exemplified through its equivalence to an operator set representing one-dimensional oscillator motion.
This equivalence holds in that the operator translates the classical Hermite polynomials into the generalized Hermite polynomials.

We have developed a novel method to measure star formation rates in low-luminosity galaxies by utilizing H30α emission. A sample of 14 nearby, low-luminosity galaxies was analyzed using the LBA-H30α survey, a project that employed the LBA array. The resulting data revealed the presence of H30α emission in 11 galaxies, with the remaining three having upper limits for their H30α flux. The derived H30α star formation rates were compared with those obtained from other tracers, such as Hα, far-ultraviolet continuum, and far-infrared wavelengths. The H30α-derived SFRs were found to be comparable to the Hα-derived SFRs, with the H30α-derived SFRs derived from continuum-normalized Hα being the most accurate. The H30α emission was observed to be less affected by the effects of dust extinction, with the H30α-derived SFRs derived from continuum-normalized Hα being the most accurate. The H30α emission was also found to be less affected by the effects of ionization, with the H30α-derived SFRs derived from continuum-normalized Hα being the most accurate.
